sm: Albert Mohler opens the Wednesday, November 11, 2026 edition by warning about a draft bill in Britain called the Conversion Practices Draft Bill, brought by the Labour government. He says it is aimed at so-called conversion therapies and would criminalize anything short of full affirmation of sexual orientation or transgender identity. He argues parents, pastors and priests could face criminal charges for ordinary conversations, and notes the Church of England has raised alarms about pastoral integrity and religious liberty. He says the bill began under Keir Starmer and is continuing under Prime Minister Andy Burnham, and he reads the bill's definition of conversion practice. He cites Telegraph coverage reporting prison terms of up to five years, and says some legal voices suggest even longer.

Mohler continues, saying the word conversion is used for propaganda value and that the bill would criminalize conversations a pastor or parent ought to have. He cites the Telegraph's point that parents could be prosecuted for restricting a child's online access or for refusing to go along with a child who identifies as a cat, and he walks through a hypothetical case of a father who limits his thirteen-year-old son's internet use. He argues that if identity is a personal project, there is no principled limit, and that the bill threatens Christian parents, teachers and pastors. He then notes the opposition is not only conservative: Richard Dawkins backed the Telegraph's campaign, calling gender as opposed to sex an anti-scientific myth.

Mohler says Dawkins holds that parents and teachers have a duty to teach a boy the scientific truth that he is a boy. He compares this odd alignment to opposition to pornography shared by conservative believers and radical feminists, and says even evolutionary biologists see that confusing male and female undermines reproduction. He cites former chief prosecutor Lord Macdonald, who told the Telegraph the bill is so unclear that parents could not tell whether an honest conversation is a crime punishable by up to five years, making it contrary to the rule of law. He says this is government legislation, not a private member's bill, and describes how moral revolutions move from tolerated, to right, to enforced. He then turns to the American midterms, where voters in Arizona, Nebraska, Colorado and Washington backed keeping girls' teams for biological females.

Mohler says many of those voters also backed candidates who hold the opposite view, citing Nicole Russell of USA Today, and he uses Texas as an example, naming James Talarico as senator-elect. He says Democrats will soon control Congress and will have to face these issues. He cites Rahm Emanuel's Wall Street Journal piece arguing Democrats ignore the voters' message at their peril, because the vote was anti-Trump rather than pro-Democrat. Mohler doubts that argument will gain traction, pointing to the many Democratic Socialists of America members elected and to Senator-elect Osseyad of Michigan. He closes by saying that for Christian churches and families, these questions are settled by God's Word and creation order, and are not up for legislative or referendum vote.
